activities.caption: file each phrase: weather or climate
activities.name: lcWeatherSort

config.prompt: London and Beijing share one and not the other — file each phrase:

items.label: the average of weather over about 30 years
how variable, how extreme, how seasonal

config.why: Climate is the stage; weather is the improvisation on it — which is why two cities can share an average while their day-to-day behaves utterly differently.

activities.anchor: Climate itself is mostly a geometry story
activities.caption: call the equator's wattage
activities.name: lcEquatorEstimate

config.prompt: At equinox, roughly how many watts per square metre does the equator average?
config.why: About 433 — with the poles getting essentially nothing: the same beam spread over more and more ground, plus a longer path through the atmosphere. The tropics receive roughly twice the solar power of the poles, and almost every climate map is downstream of that fact.

activities.anchor: The geometry is precise enough to calculate
activities.caption: pin London's noon sun at equinox
activities.name: lcNoonPlace

config.prompt: At equinox in London (51.5°N), the noon sun stands at what angle above the horizon?
config.why: 90° − |51.5 − 0| = 38.5° — the rule: noon sun angle = 90° minus the absolute difference between your latitude and the sun's declination. Above the circles at 66.5°, the angle goes negative for part of the year — the polar night.

activities.caption: design a planet — upright or tilted?
activities.name: lcPlanetBranch

config.root: You are designing a planet and must set its axial tilt.

choices.label: Upright — zero tilt
choices.feedback: All year becomes the average day: latitude alone decides the climate, and seasons vanish everywhere.

choices.label: Lean it 23.4°
choices.feedback: Each hemisphere takes turns leaning into the light — noon sun height and day length stack, and the yearly rhythm that ecosystems and agriculture are built around appears.

end.text: Earth's 23.4° sits in the Goldilocks middle — strong enough for a yearly rhythm, mild enough to keep most of the planet habitable.

config.why: Seasons are a tilt phenomenon, not a distance phenomenon — Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, the depth of northern winter. Mercury (0.03°) has almost no seasons; Uranus, tipped 98°, gives each pole 42 years of daylight followed by 42 of dark.

activities.caption: true or false — the tilt dossier
activities.name: lcTiltJudge

statements.s: Mercury's axis barely tilts (0.03°), so it has almost no seasons.
statements.why: No lean, no yearly rhythm — latitude is the whole story.

statements.s: Uranus is tipped 98° — rolling around its orbit — giving each pole 42 years of daylight followed by 42 of dark.
statements.why: The extreme end of the tilt dial.

statements.s: Seasons come from Earth swinging closer to the Sun in July.
statements.why: The gap between perihelion and aphelion is only about 3 per cent of the orbital distance, and perihelion lands in early January — the geometry argues the wrong way.

statements.s: June in one half of the world is December in the other.
statements.why: The two hemispheres take turns leaning into the light.

activities.anchor: because it receives the most solar power
activities.caption: drag the divider — who actually roasts
activities.name: lcRoastCompare

config.prompt: 'The place with the most sunshine must be the hottest' — drag the divider:

before.label: The equator's budget
before.text: It takes more energy but spends much of it evaporating water under near-daily thunderclouds — the result is steadiness, not records.

after.label: The desert belts at 25–35°
after.text: Descending air, cloudless skies and dry ground — the surface roasts, which is where the reliably hottest readings sit: Death Valley, the Sahara.

config.why: Tropical climates are warm and steady, not extreme — the reliably hottest air temperatures sit in the subtropical deserts, the Hadley engine's downdraught at full power.

activities.anchor: reading four of them is a complete tour
activities.caption: pair each station with its graph personality
activities.name: lcGraphMatch

config.prompt: Four archetypes — pair each station with its chart:

pairs.right: temperature flat near 27 °C all year; tall, near-uniform rain columns — the tropical rainforest climate
line arcs ~5 °C to ~18 °C; moderate columns with a slight autumn peak — temperate maritime, watered by the westerlies
warm line, rain columns a cliff — near-zero for eight months, then 700+ mm in July: the monsoon
warm line, columns nearly empty — the subtropical desert under the Hadley cell's descending air

config.why: The diagnostic questions are always the same: what is the temperature range (continentality), when does the rain fall (pressure belts), and how much in the wettest month (how hard the engine is running overhead)?

activities.anchor: One complication deserves full section status
activities.caption: the trades slacken — watch two coasts
activities.name: lcNinoBranch

config.root: Every two to seven years the Pacific trade winds slacken and the warm pool sloshes east. Pick a coast.

choices.label: Peru
choices.feedback: The cold upwelling fails — the anchovy fishery collapses and the coastal deserts flood.

choices.label: The western Pacific
choices.feedback: Australia and Indonesia tip into drought and fire, the Indian monsoon weakens, and Atlantic hurricanes are suppressed.

end.text: The globe's average temperature steps up a notch — the record years 1998, 2016 and 2023–24 were all El Niño years.

config.why: El Niño redistributes heat and rain; its global-average bump is a wobble riding on the warming trend, not the trend itself — and La Niña, its mirror-image sister, roughly reverses the pattern.
